cues.text: A Single Ancient Witness
Almost everything known about Tarcisius with real historical confidence comes from four lines of Latin verse.
Sometime in the later fourth century, Pope St. Damasus I composed a short epigram in his honor, comparing him directly to the protomartyr St. Stephen .
Just as Stephen was stoned by a hostile crowd, Damasus wrote, so Tarcisius was set upon by a mob while carrying the Blessed Sacrament.
He died rather than surrender 'the Sacred Body' to what the pope called 'the raging dogs.'
Damasus does not say when this happened, how old Tarcisius was, or even whether he was an acolyte or already a deacon.
He says only that Rome, a little over a century after the fact, still remembered a boy who chose death over letting the Eucharist he carried fall into profane hands.
A Story Filled In By Later Centuries
Everything more specific that later ages came to believe about Tarcisius rests on tradition considerably later and less secure than Damasus's own testimony.
These claims include that he was twelve years old and lived under the persecution of the Emperor Valerian around the year 257.

They also include that he volunteered at Mass to carry Communion to imprisoned Christians because no deacon could safely go, and that his killers were former childhood playmates who turned on him when they discovered what he carried.
A sixth-century account of the martyrdom of Pope St. Stephen I adds that Tarcisius served as the pope's own acolyte.
This would explain why so delicate and dangerous a mission fell to him in particular, though this too postdates Tarcisius's own era by roughly three hundred years.
A Novelist's Gift to the Story

Devotion to Tarcisius, real enough in ancient Rome to earn him a papal epigram, found an unexpected new audience in 1854, when Cardinal Nicholas Wiseman wove his martyrdom into Fabiola, a popular novel of Christian life in the catacombs.

Wiseman's vivid, deliberately moving account of the boy's final walk through Rome, hosts hidden against his heart, shaped how generations of Catholics have pictured Tarcisius ever since — more, in fact, than any ancient source actually describes.

It is worth being clear about that debt: much of the emotional detail Catholics associate with Tarcisius today is nineteenth-century fiction inspired by an ancient epigram, not ancient testimony in its own right.
Body and Relics
Later tradition holds that Tarcisius's body was recovered and carried to the catacombs of St. Callixtus.
There Pope Sixtus II received it and offered Mass to mark what the Church calls a martyr's true birthday, the day of death that opens onto eternal life.

According to the same tradition, Sixtus governed Rome during these same years of persecution and would himself be martyred not long after, alongside his deacons, who are commemorated with him as Sixtus II and Companions .
Relics venerated under his name are today claimed by the church of San Silvestro in Capite in Rome.
Yet the chain connecting them with certainty to the boy Damasus once eulogized cannot be traced in unbroken historical detail, as with so much of his story.
Legacy
Pope Benedict XVI addressed a vast pilgrimage of altar servers in 2010 and held Tarcisius up as exactly the model their office still calls for.

He presented him not simply as a boy from a distant century, but as a witness to what it means to guard something entrusted to unworthy, ordinary hands with a seriousness that does not waver even under threat.
His feast falls on 15 August, all but eclipsed on the calendar by the Assumption.
This quiet placement seems, in its own way, fitting for a saint remembered less for his life’s details than for the single, complete thing he refused to give up.
We recognize in Tarcisius a witness that courage is not reserved for the old or the powerful.
A child entrusted with something sacred can, when the moment comes, guard it with a resolve that adults twice his age might envy.
